source.title: Can Open-source LLMs Enhance Data Augmentation for Toxic Detection?: An Experimental Study
source.authors: Zheng Hui; Zhaoxiao Guo; Hang Zhao; Juanyong Duan; Lin Ai; Yinheng Li; Julia Hirschberg; Congrui Huang

record.file_problem: None noted. Table 2 is flattened in the supplied text, so its percentages cannot be reliably assigned to individual models.
record.tranche_reason: The study treats safety alignment as an obstacle to generating toxic data and uses supervised fine-tuning to improve that generation for a separate data-augmentation purpose. It does not test the claim versions' specified safety behaviours or mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports frequent prompt-time refusals for toxic data-generation requests and limited success from changing prompts. Its fine-tuning is expressly intended to elicit toxic data, so the resulting generation is not evidence that safety behaviour generally disappears after fine-tuning. The supplied Table 2 percentages cannot be mapped reliably to models, and the fine-tuning tables primarily report downstream classifier metrics rather than refusal or harmful-request compliance rates.
record.test_reason: The paper deliberately fine-tunes Mistral/Vicuna/Mixtral with LoRA on harmful-content datasets so they generate toxic training data. It reports only downstream classifier F1/accuracy and duplication rates, never refusal or harmful-request compliance rates before and after fine-tuning. The fine-tuning induces the behaviour on purpose and does not measure it. Prompt-time refusals (Gemma, Bloom) and the limited success of prompt edits are related observations that measure no version's construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that prompt engineering is limited by built-in safety mechanisms. They find that LoRA fine-tuning improves diversity, realism and downstream detection, making fine-tuned open models (notably Mistral) cost-effective near-GPT-4 alternatives. They also note that fine-tuning brings overfitting and duplication in later epochs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses LoRA supervised fine-tuning on harmful-content datasets to generate toxic examples for data augmentation; it does not reproduce the cited safety-compromising fine-tuning method or measure refusal removal.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report limited success from changes to few-shot examples and requirement specificity. They also state that prompt-version choice has minimal impact on downstream fine-tuned classifier performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Under prompt-only toxic-data-generation requests, Gemma-7B refused hate content outright and Bloom-7B/LLaMA-7B/13B had ≤10% valid hate samples (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-aligned open models often refuse prompt-based requests to synthesize hate speech, with refusal varying by model and harm category.

fits_no_version.finding: Editing few-shot examples and requirement specificity gave limited success in bypassing safety mechanisms.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-template edits alone rarely bypass refusal for toxic data synthesis.

record.problems: For the safety-related findings, refusal frequency is qualitative and no refusal rates or post-fine-tuning harmful-request compliance rates are reported. The relevant model-level percentages in Table 2 are flattened and cannot be assigned reliably from the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. The fine-tuning results in Tables 3, 4, and 7 primarily measure downstream toxic-content classifier performance, not safety refusal or harmful-request compliance. The model success-rate entries in Table 2 were not assigned because the supplied flattened layout does not support reliable mapping.

untested.parts: Refusal or harmful-request compliance rates after LoRA fine-tuning on harmful data. Fine-tuning was intended to elicit toxic text, and only classifier metrics are reported.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes. The AOA role prompt in Appendix A is used but its effect on refusal is not reported.

record.verdict_notes: The record's claim that Table 2 cannot be mapped is overly cautious. Read row by row, the flattened text gives political/hate success per model: LLaMA-7B ≥65%/≤10%, LLaMA-13B ≥85%/≤10%, Vicuna ≥70%/≥85%, Mistral ≥85%/≥85%, Falcon ≥60%/≤30%, Bloom ≥60%/≤10%, Gemma ≥50%/Reject. These figures still bear on no version. The paper cites Qi et al. (2310.03693) for data mixing and uses an AOA-style jailbreak prompt, but measures no safety outcome.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples removes refusal to harmful user requests, and by how much.
Whether benign fine-tuning raises harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Whether compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether the training data or objective causes safety to be shallow.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond early response tokens deepens safety and whether that effect persists.

rows.subject: Gemma

conditions.value: Generate toxic content for data augmentation

rows.note: The paper groups Gemma with Bloom as models whose safety alignments led to frequent refusals; it gives no model-specific refusal rate.
rows.check: Value can be sharpened. Table 2 is readable in order: Gemma-7B is 'Reject to Answer' on hate prompts and ≥50% success on political prompts. This is a prompt-only refusal and bears on no version.

rows.subject: Bloom

conditions.value: Generate toxic content for data augmentation

rows.note: The paper groups Bloom with Gemma as models whose safety alignments led to frequent refusals; it gives no model-specific refusal rate.
rows.check: Table 2 gives Bloom-7B hate success ≤10% and political ≥60%, consistent with frequent refusal on hate. This is a prompt-only observation and bears on no version.

rows.subject: Six open-source LLMs (aggregate; individual models not identified for this statement)
rows.operation_detail: Tested prompt-template, few-shot-example, and requirement-specificity changes

conditions.value: Bypass safety mechanisms to generate harmful data
Altered few-shot examples and requirement specificity

rows.measure: Success of prompt changes in bypassing safety mechanisms
rows.note: The statement reports the prompt-engineering stage in aggregate and does not give separate outcomes for each model or prompt.
rows.check: The prompt changes are few-shot and requirement-specificity edits, not prefill, suffix or decoding attacks, so the row does not bear on V4. 'Limited success' is qualitative and has no baseline, so 'partial' is not meaningful here.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
